title: Ang 83–91: Sri Rag ki Var

segments.voice: Some songs land in your chest before you've caught a single word: a drumline, a crowd chanting a name, a bhangra beat rolling out of a passing car. You feel the rhythm first and the meaning second. So why would a book of hymns hold a ballad? On ang 83 the Granth turns to its first var: a ballad, built to be sung, with a beat you could tap on your knee.
screen: `A BEAT FROM A PASSING CAR.` → `RHYTHM FIRST, MEANING SECOND.` → `THE FIRST VAR.`

segments.voice: Sri Rag ki Var is Guru Ram Das's ballad, and it moves in two voices. The pauris are its stanzas, his own, each one a step forward. Before each pauri come saloks, short verses, some by other Gurus, set in front like a call before the answer. Short, then full. Salok, then pauri. Once you hear the pattern, you can feel it coming. The very first salok, on ang 83, is by Guru Amar Das, and it's about music itself. In paraphrase: among the ragas, Sri Rag is the best, if through it you come to love the True One. Notice the if. The finest music counts when it carries love. Without that, it's only a lovely sound. And the hero of this ballad isn't a warrior riding into battle. The pauris praise the One, the Creator who made the world and watches over it. So the Granth borrows the ballad's drive, the beat that makes you lean in, and points it somewhere new. At the gurdwara, ragis sing it with harmonium and tabla, and the room feels the rhythm before it catches every word. That's the senses doing their job: the beat carries you to the meaning.
screen: `TWO VOICES: SALOK, THEN PAURI.` · `SRI RAG IS BEST, IF IT CARRIES LOVE.` · `THE HERO IS THE ONE.` · `THE BEAT CARRIES THE MEANING.` · then, large: `THE FIRST VAR.`

segments.voice: Find a salok near ang 84 in a Gurbani app, or use today's: among the ragas, Sri Rag is the best, if it carries love for the True One. Say it once in a low voice and tap the beat on your knee as you go. Then stop tapping, and let whatever sound is in the room, a fan, traffic, your own breath, carry the rest of the sit.

First salok of Sri Rag ki Var (Mahala 3): 'among the ragas Sri Rag is the best, if through it one enshrines love for the True One'. The 'best' is the text's own word, so the superlative is kept and attributed. Confirm attribution and Ang.
'The pauris praise the One, the Creator who made the world and watches over it': a general description of this var's pauris; confirm.

Var described as 'a ballad, built to be sung'; the history of vars as heroic ballads in Punjabi is only implied (hook and trapdoor), not stated as fact. Confirm the trapdoor's 'the saloks before them were set in from other Gurus' (attributed to Guru Arjan's compiling in standard accounts; left unattributed here).
